nodes.label: Apply the exponent laws
nodes.description: Simplify exponential expressions without a calculator by applying the product, quotient and power laws together with the zero and negative exponent identities.

nodes.label: Reduce to prime bases
nodes.description: Simplify exponential expressions whose terms have different bases by reducing the bases to prime bases and then applying the exponent laws.

nodes.label: Factorise exponential expressions
nodes.description: Simplify exponential fractions with more than one term by factorising, taking out a common factor or using the difference of squares, and cancelling.

nodes.label: Simplify expressions with rational exponents
nodes.description: Simplify expressions with rational exponents, including products and quotients of powers and rational powers of products, by applying the exponent laws

nodes.label: Evaluate numeric rational powers
nodes.description: Evaluate, without a calculator, a number raised to a rational exponent, including a decimal base or a negative rational exponent, by rewriting the base as a fraction or a prime power.

nodes.label: Equate exponents, same base
nodes.description: Solve an exponential equation by writing both sides as a single power of the same base (changing to prime bases and using a^0 = 1 where needed) and equating the exponents.

nodes.label: Take out common factor
nodes.description: Solve an exponential equation containing terms with different exponents of the same base by rewriting the terms, taking out the common factor, simplifying and then equating exponents.

nodes.label: Solve by factorising
nodes.description: Solve an exponential equation that reduces to a trinomial, a difference of two squares or a product of factors equal to zero by rewriting and factorising, solving each factor and rejecting factors that cannot be satisfied.

nodes.label: Trial and error estimates
nodes.description: Use trial and error to find the value of x, correct to 2 decimal places, in an exponential equation whose sides cannot be written with the same base.

solution: Change the bases to prime numbers: At first glance it appears that we cannot simplify this expression. However, if we reduce the bases to prime bases, then we can apply the exponent laws. $\dfrac{{2}^{2n}\times{4}^{n}\times2}{{16}^{n}}=\dfrac{{2}^{2n}\times{\left({2}^{2}\right)}^{n}\times{2}^{1}}{{\left({2}^{4}\right)}^{n}}$

Change the bases to prime numbers: $\begin{aligned}\dfrac{{5}^{2x-1}\cdot{9}^{x-2}}{{15}^{2x-3}}&=\dfrac{{5}^{2x-1}\cdot{\left({3}^{2}\right)}^{x-2}}{{\left(5\times3\right)}^{2x-3}}\\&=\dfrac{{5}^{2x-1}\cdot{3}^{2x-4}}{{5}^{2x-3}\cdot{3}^{2x-3}}\end{aligned}$
Write the answer as a fraction: $\begin{aligned}&=\frac{5^{2}}{3}\\&=\frac{25}{3}\end{aligned}$

Simplify to a form that can be factorised: For each of the exponent laws we can “undo” the law - in other words we can work backwards. For this expression we can reverse the multiplication law to write $2^{t-2}$ as $2^{t}\cdot2^{-2}$ . $\frac{{2}^{t}-{2}^{t-2}}{3\cdot{2}^{t}-{2}^{t}}=\frac{{2}^{t}-\left({2}^{t}\cdot{2}^{-2}\right)}{3\cdot{2}^{t}-{2}^{t}}$
Cancel the common factor and simplify: $\begin{aligned}&=\frac{1-2^{-2}}{3-1}\\&=\frac{1-\frac{1}{4}}{2}\\&=\frac{3}{4}\times\frac{1}{2}\\&=\frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}$

Change the bases to prime numbers: $\begin{aligned}\frac{9^{x}-1}{3^{x}+1}&=\frac{\left(3^{2}\right)^{x}-1}{3^{x}+1}\\&=\frac{3^{2x}-1}{3^{x}+1}\quad\text{Recognisethat}3^{2x}=\left(3^{x}\right)^{2}\end{aligned}$
Factorise using the difference of squares: $=\dfrac{\left({3}^{x}-1\right)\left({3}^{x}+1\right)}{{3}^{x}+1}$
Cancel the common factor and simplify: $={3}^{x}-1$

questions.stem: If $2^{2013}.5^{2015}$ is written out in full how many digits will there be?

solution: Write as a fraction and simplify: $\begin{aligned}(\text{0.008})^{\frac{1}{3}}&=\left(\frac{8}{1000}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\\&=\left(\frac{1}{125}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\\&=\left(\frac{1}{5^{3}}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\\&=\frac{1^{\frac{1}{3}}}{5^{\left(3\cdot\frac{1}{3}\right)}}\\&=\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}$
Change the bases to prime numbers: ${3}^{x+1}={3}^{2}$
The bases are the same so we can equate exponents: $\begin{aligned}x+1&=2\\\therefore x&=1\end{aligned}$
Solve for: We know from the exponent identities that $a^{0}=1$ , therefore: $\begin{aligned}3^{t}&=1\\3^{t}&=3^{0}\\\therefore t&=0\end{aligned}$
Change the bases to prime numbers: ${5}^{t}={5}^{2}$
The bases are the same so we can equate exponents: $\therefore t=2$
Solve for: $3^x=81$ or $3^x=-1$ . However $3^x=-1$ is undefined, so: $\begin{aligned}3^{x}&=81\\3^{x}&=3^{4}\\x&=4\end{aligned}$ Therefore $x=4$
Rewrite the equation: We notice that ${\left({p}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)}^{2}=p$ so we can rewrite the equation as: ${\left({p}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)}^{2}-13{p}^{\frac{1}{2}}+36=0$

Solve to find both roots: $\begin{aligned}p^{\frac{1}{2}}-9&=0&\text{or}&&p^{\frac{1}{2}}-4&=0\\p^{\frac{1}{2}}&=9&&&p^{\frac{1}{2}}&=4\\\left(p^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{2}&=(9)^{2}&&&\left(p^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{2}&=(4)^{2}\\p&=81&&&p&=16\end{aligned}$ Therefore $p=81$ or $p=16$ .

Rewrite the equation: In order to get the equation into a form which we can factorise, we need to rewrite the equation: $\begin{aligned}2^{x}-2^{4-x}&=0\\2^{x}-2^{4}\cdot2^{-x}&=0\\2^{x}-\frac{2^{4}}{2^{x}}&=0\end{aligned}$ Now eliminate the fraction by multiplying both sides of the equation by the denominator, $2^{x}$ . $\begin{aligned}\left(2^{x}-\frac{2^{4}}{2^{x}}\right)\times2^{x}&=0\times2^{x}\\2^{2x}-16&=0\end{aligned}$

Factorise the equation: Now that we have rearranged the equation, we can see that we are left with a difference of two squares. Therefore: $\begin{aligned}2^{2x}-16&=0\\(2^{x}-4)(2^{x}+4)&=0\\2^{x}&=4&\qquad2^{x}\neq-4\quad\text{(apositiveintegerwithanexponentisalwayspositive)}\\2^{x}=2^{2}&=4\\x&=2\end{aligned}$ Therefore $x=2$ .

content.text_md: Explain why the following statements are false: $\dfrac{1}{a^{-1}+b^{-1}}=a+b$
The sum of two powers of the same degree is not the power of the sum of the bases
Explain why the following statements are false: $(a+b)^2=a^2+b^2$
The sum of two powers of the same degree is not the power of the sum of the bases
Explain why the following statements are false: $2.3^x=6^x$
We cannot multiply bases unless they are raised to the same power
Explain why the following statements are false: $(3x^4y^2)^3=3x^{12}y^6$
The power of a product is the product of all the bases raised to the same power
Explain why the following statements are false: $\left(\frac{1}{a^2}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}=a^{\frac{2}{3}}$
A negative sign is missing, when a power is moved from the denominator to the numerator, the sign of the exponent changes. From the question we must note that $a\neq0$
Explain why the following statements are false: $x^{-\frac{1}{2}}=\dfrac{1}{-x^{\frac{1}{2}}}$
The sign of a base is not changed when an exponent is moved from the denominator to the numerator in a fraction

claims.claim: Product law: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents.
Quotient law: a^m / a^n = a^(m-n), dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents.
Power of a product: (ab)^n = a^n b^n.
Power of a quotient: (a/b)^n = a^n / b^n.
Power law: (a^m)^n = a^(mn), raising a power to a power multiplies the exponents.
The exponent laws as listed hold where a > 0, b > 0 and m, n are real numbers.
To multiply powers of the same base, write the base once and add the exponents: 2^(3x) × 2^(4x) = 2^(3x+4x) = 2^(7x).
To divide terms with coefficients and powers, divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents of the same variable: 4x^3 / 2x^5 = 2x^(3-5).
A factor with a negative exponent is written in the denominator with the positive exponent: 2x^(-2) = 2 / x^2.
With several variables, divide the numerical coefficients and subtract the exponents of each variable separately: 12p^2 t^5 / 3p t^3 = 4p^(2-1) t^(5-3) = 4p t^2.
To raise a product to a power, raise each factor to that power: (3x)^2 = 3^2 x^2 = 9x^2.
To raise a product of powers to a power, multiply each exponent by the outer exponent: (3^4 × 5^2)^3 = 3^(4×3) × 5^(2×3) = 3^12 × 5^6.
Zero exponent: each power with exponent 0 is replaced by 1, so 6p^0 × (7p)^0 = 6(1) × 1 = 6.
To simplify a fraction raised to a power, first simplify the fraction inside the brackets, then raise numerator and denominator to the power: (2xp / 6x^2)^3 = (p / 3x)^3 = p^3 / 27x^3.
To raise a power to a power with a negative exponent, multiply the exponents, expanding the bracket: (2^(-2))^(2x+1) = 2^(-2(2x+1)) = 2^(-4x-2).
When a fraction is one term over one term, use the method of Finding Prime Bases, that is, use prime factorisation on the bases.
An expression whose terms have different bases may seem impossible to simplify, but if the bases are reduced to prime bases the exponent laws can be applied.
Change each base to a prime base: 4^n is written as (2^2)^n, 16^n as (2^4)^n, and the lone factor 2 as 2^1.
Simplify a power of a power by multiplying the exponents: (2^2)^n becomes 2^(2n) and (2^4)^n becomes 2^(4n).
Multiply powers of the same base in the numerator by adding the exponents: 2^(2n) × 2^(2n) × 2^1 = 2^(2n+2n+1) = 2^(4n+1).
Divide powers of the same base by subtracting the exponents: 2^(4n+1) / 2^(4n) = 2^(4n+1-(4n)), which gives 2.
Change the bases to primes: 9 is written as 3^2, giving (3^2)^(x-2), and 15 is written as 5 × 3, giving (5×3)^(2x-3).
A power of a power is simplified by multiplying the exponents: (3^2)^(x-2) becomes 3^(2x-4).
A power of a product of prime bases is split by applying the exponent to each prime base: (5×3)^(2x-3) becomes 5^(2x-3) · 3^(2x-3).
Subtract the exponents for each base separately, the powers of 5 with the powers of 5 and the powers of 3 with the powers of 3.
When subtracting exponents, remove the brackets and change the signs of the subtracted exponent: (2x-1)-(2x-3) = 2x-1-2x+3 = 2.
Write the answer as a fraction: a negative exponent is moved to the denominator, so 5^2 × 3^(-1) = 5^2 / 3 = 25/3.
Change the base to a prime base: 9^x is written as (3^2)^x and simplified to 3^(2x).
When working with exponents, all the laws of operation for algebra apply.
When a fraction has more than one term in the numerator or denominator, change to prime bases if necessary and then factorise.
Each exponent law can be undone, that is, worked backwards, to make an expression factorisable.
Reverse the multiplication law to write 2^(t-2) as 2^t · 2^(-2), so that 2^t appears in every term.
Take out the common factor 2^t in the numerator and in the denominator: (2^t − 2^t · 2^(-2)) / (3 · 2^t − 2^t) = 2^t(1 − 2^(-2)) / 2^t(3 − 1).
Cancel the common factor 2^t, leaving (1 − 2^(-2)) / (3 − 1).
After cancelling, evaluate the negative power numerically: 2^(-2) = 1/4, giving (1 − 1/4) / 2.
Simplify the resulting numerical fraction: (1 − 1/4) / 2 is written as 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8.
Recognise that 3^(2x) = (3^x)^2, so the numerator 3^(2x) − 1 has the form of a difference of two squares.
Factorise the numerator using the difference of squares: 3^(2x) − 1 = (3^x − 1)(3^x + 1).
Cancel the common factor (3^x + 1) from numerator and denominator, leaving 3^x − 1.
The exponent laws can also be applied to expressions with rational exponents.
To simplify a product of powers of the same base with rational exponents, add the exponents: in 2x^(1/2) × 4x^(-1/2) the powers of x combine as x^(1/2 - 1/2).
When simplifying 2x^(1/2) × 4x^(-1/2), the coefficients 2 and 4 are multiplied to give 8.
Adding the exponents 1/2 and -1/2 gives the exponent 0, so 2x^(1/2) × 4x^(-1/2) becomes 8x^0.
A power with exponent 0 is replaced by 1, so 8x^0 = 8(1) = 8.
To simplify a decimal base raised to a rational exponent, write the base as a fraction and simplify it.
The decimal 0.008 is written as the fraction 8/1000, so (0.008)^(1/3) = (8/1000)^(1/3).
A rational exponent on a fraction is applied to the numerator and to the denominator separately: (1/5^3)^(1/3) = 1^(1/3) / 5^(3 · 1/3).
A power raised to a rational exponent has its exponents multiplied: (5^3)^(1/3) = 5^(3 · 1/3).
Evaluating by this method gives (0.008)^(1/3) = 1/5.
The book writes a decimal number with a comma as the decimal separator, for example 0.008.
The denominator 125 is rewritten as the prime power 5^3, so (1/125)^(1/3) = (1/5^3)^(1/3).
An exponential equation is an equation that has the unknown variable in the exponent.
If a single term with the same base can be written on each side of an exponential equation, the exponents can be equated; this is one method for solving exponential equations.
The rule for equating exponents holds when the base a satisfies a > 0 and a is not equal to 1.
If a^x = a^y (same base), then x = y.
If the base a = 1, then x and y can be different, so the exponents cannot be equated.
To solve 3^(x+1) = 9, change the bases to prime numbers by writing 9 as 3^2, so that 3^(x+1) = 3^2.
Once the bases are the same, equate the exponents and solve the resulting equation: x + 1 = 2, therefore x = 1.
From the exponent identities, a^0 = 1.
To solve 3^t = 1, write the 1 as a power of the same base using a^0 = 1, so 3^t = 3^0, and equate the exponents to get t = 0.
When terms have different exponents of the same base, as in 5^t + 3.5^(t+1) = 400, first rewrite the term with the different exponent: 5^(t+1) is written as 5^t . 5.
Take out the common factor 5^t, giving 5^t(1 + 3.5) = 400, which becomes 5^t(1 + 15) = 400.
Simplify the bracket and the equation to leave a single power: 5^t(16) = 400 gives 5^t = 25.
Change the bases to prime numbers by writing 25 as 5^2, so 5^t = 5^2, then equate the exponents (same base) to get t = 2.
To solve 3^(2x) - 80.3^x - 81 = 0, factorise the trinomial: (3^x - 81)(3^x + 1) = 0.
Solve each factor by setting it equal to zero, giving 3^x = 81 or 3^x = -1.
3^x = -1 is undefined, so that factor is rejected and only 3^x = 81 is kept.
For the remaining factor, write 81 as 3^4 so 3^x = 3^4, then equate the exponents to get x = 4.
When an equation such as p - 13p^(1/2) + 36 = 0 is not yet in factorisable form, notice that (p^(1/2))^2 = p and rewrite it as (p^(1/2))^2 - 13p^(1/2) + 36 = 0.
Factorise the rewritten equation as a trinomial: (p^(1/2) - 9)(p^(1/2) - 4) = 0.
Solve each factor to find both roots: set p^(1/2) - 9 = 0 and p^(1/2) - 4 = 0, then square both sides of each (for example (p^(1/2))^2 = 9^2) to get p = 81 or p = 16.
Both roots are the solution: p = 81 or p = 16.
To solve 2^x - 2^(4-x) = 0, first rewrite the equation into a form that can be factorised: 2^(4-x) = 2^4 . 2^(-x) = 2^4 / 2^x.
Eliminate the fraction by multiplying both sides of the equation by the denominator, 2^x, which gives 2^(2x) - 16 = 0.
The rearranged equation 2^(2x) - 16 = 0 is a difference of two squares and factorises as (2^x - 4)(2^x + 4) = 0.
2^x = -4 is rejected because a positive integer with an exponent is always positive; only 2^x = 4 = 2^2 is kept, so x = 2.
